newsitem.title: UK: British insurer ups direct motor rates.
newsitem.headline: British insurer ups direct motor rates.

text.p: Guardian Direct, a leading British direct motor insurer, said on Thursday it has over recent weeks dramatically increased the prices it charges customers for motor cover.
But in a saturated market, which at best is only just coming out of a deep pricing trough, and where competition remains fierce, big industry wide price rises may still be some way off.

Ray Pierce, managing director of Guardian Direct, the direct selling personal motor insurance arm of British composite Guardian Royal Exchange, said the last few months had seen a sustained rise in personal motor premium rates across much of the direct sales sector.

He said that Guardian Direct, which has 650,000 customers or around three percent of the entire British motor insurance market and which in April bought RAC (Royal Automobile Club) Insurance Brokers, had increased base premium rates for personal motor insurance policies by over 10 percent since June.
Retentions were holding at over eighty percent, he added.

Guardian said at the interim results stage in July that it had put through selective price increases of up to five percent on motor policies and expected to see rises of up to seven percent in direct motor rates over the course of the next year.
"Everybody in the direct market is now on average pushing up their prices," Pierce said. "There has been an increase in the latter part of the year."
Guardian's biggest rival, Royal Bank of Scotland's Direct Line Insurance, which sells more motor policies than any insurer in Britain, said the price rises were not unexpected.
But the insurer added that it had not put through baseline increases of anything approaching the 10 percent level and many industry analysts still remained sceptical of a widespread upturn.
"We have said for a long time the pricing in the market was unsustainable and that price rises, consolidation and withdrawals were inevitable," chief executive Ian Chippendale said.

"We are making small selective increases but we suggest that over the next 18 months those increases are not going to amount to more than two to three percent," added spokesman Adrian Webb. "The overall state of motor premium rates in the industry is that people are losing money."

Intense competition in Britain's overcrowded insurance sector has pushed personal motor premiums down by around 20 percent over the last two years. Several insurers have this year provided evidence of a very modest and selective rebound, but it remained to be seen how sustained or far reaching this will be.

The direct motor market is the frontline of industry pricing. There is no intermediary between insurer and customer, so the information flow is cleaner, which means the insurer can react quickly to changing market conditions.
